validated_results.title: Calcium and fructose intake in relation to risk of prostate cancer.
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort of 47,781 men reporting multivariate relative risks for calcium intake and incident advanced prostate cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest vs lowest calcium intake category (>=2000 mg/day versus <500 mg/day)
extraction.population: Men in the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study free of cancer in 1986

sample_size.excerpt: We thus conducted a prospective study among 47,781 men of the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study free of cancer in 1986 to examine whether calcium and fructose intake influenced risk of prostate cancer. Between 1986 and 1994, 1369 non-stage A1 and 423 advanced (extraprostatic) cases of prostate cancer were diagnosed.

cases.excerpt: Between 1986 and 1994, 1369 non-stage A1 and 423 advanced (extraprostatic) cases of prostate cancer were diagnosed.

effect_size.excerpt: Higher consumption of calcium was related to advanced prostate cancer [multivariate relative risk (RR), 2.97; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.61-5.50 for intakes > or = 2000 mg/day versus < 500 mg/day; P, trend, 0.002] and metastatic prostate cancer (RR, 4.57; CI, 1.88-11.1; P, trend, <0.001).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Higher consumption of calcium was related to advanced prostate cancer [multivariate relative risk (RR), 2.97; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.61-5.50 for intakes > or = 2000 mg/day versus < 500 mg/day; P, trend, 0.002] and metastatic prostate cancer (RR, 4.57; CI, 1.88-11.1; P, trend, <0.001).

validated_results.title: Prostate cancer and supplementation with alpha-tocopherol and beta-carotene: incidence and mortality in a controlled trial.
validated_results.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
validated_results.reason: Randomized controlled trial reporting beta-carotene supplementation effect on prostate cancer incidence.

extraction.comparison_type: Beta-carotene supplementation (20 mg daily) versus no beta-carotene

sample_size.excerpt: A total of 29133 male smokers aged 50-69 years from southwestern Finland were randomly assigned to receive alpha-tocopherol (50 mg), beta-carotene (20 mg), both agents, or placebo daily for 5-8 years (median, 6.1 years).

cases.excerpt: We found 246 new cases of and 62 deaths from prostate cancer during the follow-up period.

effect_size.excerpt: Among subjects receiving beta-carotene (n = 14560), prostate cancer incidence was 23% higher (95% CI = -4%-59%) and mortality was 15% higher (95% CI = -30%-89%) compared with those not receiving it (n = 14573).
